---
title: Using Python
---

Python is a programming language. To use it, you write Python code somewhere
and ask the computer to run it.

There are three places to write that code, and we will use all three in this
course:

* the **interpreter**, where you type one line at a time and see the answer
  straight away
* a **script**, a file of Python code that Python can run as a program
* a **notebook**, a page in the browser where code and notes sit together

They run the same Python. What changes is how you work with it.

## The interpreter

Type `python` at the prompt:

```session
$ python
Python 3.14.4 (main, Jun 18 2026, 14:25:02) [GCC 15.2.0] on linux
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>>
```

The first lines tell you which version of Python you are running. The last
line, `>>>`, is Python's prompt. It works like the `$` prompt in the shell:
Python is waiting for you to type something.

Type an expression and press Enter:

```session
$ python
>>> 5 + 2
7
>>> 5 * 2
10
```

Python works out the answer and prints it. No `print`, no file, no saving -
you type, it answers.

This is called the **interpreter**, or the **REPL**: it Reads what you type,
Evaluates it, Prints the result, and Loops back for the next line.

The usual arithmetic works as you would expect:

```session
>>> 7 - 3
4
>>> 10 / 4
2.5
```

And Python is happy with numbers far larger than a calculator will take:

```session
>>> 2 ** 1000

```

`**` means "to the power of". That is 2 multiplied by itself a thousand times,
printed in full - Python does not round it off or give up.

::: {.callout-tip}
Work out `2 + 3` in the interpreter. Then try `100 * 100`, and `2 ** 64`.
:::

When you are done, type `exit()` and press Enter:

```session
>>> exit()
$
```

The `$` prompt comes back - you are in the shell again. **Ctrl+D** does the
same thing.

The interpreter is for trying things out. It is quick, and nothing is kept:
close it, and everything you typed is gone. When you want to keep what you
wrote, put it in a file.

## A script

A **script** is a text file containing Python code. In this course, we will use
JupyterLab's `%%file` cell magic to create scripts:

```python
%%file hello.py
print("hello, world!")
```

We will run them from a notebook by putting `!` before the shell command:

```python
!python hello.py
```

```text
hello, world!
```

A script keeps a program that you want to run again. A later lesson develops
this way of working in detail.

## A notebook

A **notebook** is a page in your browser where code and notes live together.
You write code in a box, run it, and the answer appears right below it. The
answers stay on the page, along with whatever you wrote around them.

Start JupyterLab from the terminal:

```session
$ jupyter lab
```

Your browser opens. On the left is a list of files. There is a notebook there
already, `jupyterlab.ipynb` - open it by double-clicking.

A notebook is made of **cells**. Some hold code, some hold notes written in
Markdown. Click on a cell to put the cursor in it, and press **Shift+Enter**
to run it. The result appears underneath, and the cursor moves to the next
cell.

Work through `jupyterlab.ipynb` from the top. It will ask you to run some code,
write some notes, and try a few things out. Do them as you go - reading a
notebook without running it teaches you very little.

When you are finished, close the browser tab and press **Ctrl+C** in the
terminal to stop JupyterLab.

A notebook is for working something out and keeping a record of it: the code,
the answers, and your notes on what you were doing.

## Which one to use

| | Good for | Kept? |
|---|---|---|
| Interpreter | trying one thing out | no |
| Script | code you will run again | yes, as a `.py` file |
| Notebook | working through a problem, with notes | yes, as an `.ipynb` file |

We will use the interpreter to try small things, notebooks for most of the
classwork, and scripts for programs worth keeping.

And the one idea to carry forward: all three are the same Python. What you
learn in one works in the others.
